questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why the letter X is used to mean a kiss
Which languages have the most letters
How to write a formal business letter
questions.why: They discuss the letter X at the end of messages and where the idea of X for a kiss comes from.

questions.q: What is Rob doing at the start of the programme?
options: Trying to guess the answer to the quiz question
questions.why: Rob says words like 'EXcited' and 'EXpectations' as clues, and Neil tells him to stop his jokes.

questions.q: According to Dr Laura Wright, how long have people added Xs for kisses to letters?
questions.why: She says we've been adding Xs for kisses since at least 1763.

questions.q: How many Xs were on the first known example?
questions.why: Dr Wright says the very first one we know of had seven Xs.

questions.q: Why might X have come to mean a kiss?
options: Because it looks like two lips
Its original sound /ks/ is close to 'kiss'
Because the Romans always used it at the end of their letters
Because it was the last letter of the alphabet
questions.why: Rob says Dr Wright suggests it's because of the original pronunciation, /ks/.

questions.q: Who do people usually put an X for?
questions.why: Neil says it's usually only for friends and family, people you might kiss in real life.

questions.q: What mistake did Professor Nils Langer's German colleague make?
options: She forgot to sign her letters
She wrote all her official letters in German, not English
She put Xs on every letter, even to the tax office
questions.why: She finished any letter with Xs, 'even a letter to the Inland Revenue'.

questions.q: What does the presenter imply with his joke about the tax office?
options: They were very pleased to receive such friendly letters
They might have taken more money from her
questions.why: He joked they 'docked her another 20 quid', meaning took more money from her.
